<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 9 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Newton-Cartan Theory</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">9.3</span> Stratified Atlas</h1></header>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>To read off the physical content of Newton’s axioms, we work in charts adapted to the foliation, whose time coordinate is absolute time. A chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> is <strong>stratified</strong> if <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^0 = \left. t \right|_\mathcal{U}\)</span>, so that the absolute spaces are the slices <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^0 = \text{const}\)</span>. Stratified charts exist around every point<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-4" id="fnref-4" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 4">4</a></sup> and form the <strong>stratified atlas</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}_{\text{strat.}} \subseteq \mathcal{A}\)</span>, so we can always restrict to them. In what follows, Latin indices <span class="math inline">\(i, j, k, \dots\)</span> run over <span class="math inline">\(\{0, 1, 2, 3\}\)</span> and Greek indices <span class="math inline">\(\alpha, \beta, \delta, \dots\)</span> over <span class="math inline">\(\{1, 2, 3\}\)</span>. Between two stratified charts,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^0}{\partial \mathscr{X}^0} = 1,
            \qquad
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^0}{\partial \mathscr{X}^\beta} = 0,
            \qquad
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^\alpha}{\partial \mathscr{X}^0} \text{ arbitrary}.
        \end{align*}</span>  Stratified charts agree on when an event happens, but their spatial coordinates may move, rotate, or deform in time. See more on pseudo-forces at Section <a class="dg-xref" href="pseudo-forces.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Pseudo_Forces">9.4</a>.</p></li>
<li><p>In a stratified chart, <span class="math inline">\(\left. dt \right|_\mathcal{U} = dx^0\)</span> has constant component functions <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{t}_k = \delta^0_k\)</span>, hence <span class="math inline">\(\big( \nabla_{\partial x_i} dt \big)_k = - \Gamma^0_{ki}\)</span> and  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \nabla dt = 0
            \longleftrightarrow
            \Gamma^0_{ki} = 0 \quad \forall \, k, i.
        \end{align*}</span>  Uniform flow thus removes all connection coefficient functions with an upper time index. Of the <span class="math inline">\(40\)</span> coefficients of a torsion-free connection in four dimensions, the remaining <span class="math inline">\(30\)</span> are <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\delta} = \Gamma^\alpha_{\delta\beta}\)</span> (<span class="math inline">\(18\)</span>), <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta} = \Gamma^\alpha_{\beta0}\)</span> (<span class="math inline">\(9\)</span>) and <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\)</span> (<span class="math inline">\(3\)</span>).</p></li>
<li><p>With <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \equiv t\)</span>, so that <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U} = (t \circ \gamma)' = 1\)</span>, and the component functions <span class="math inline">\(f^k_\gamma(t) \coloneqq (dx^k)_{\gamma(t)}\big( \mathcal{F}_\gamma(t) \big)\)</span> of the force, Newton II reads <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U}(t) + \Gamma^k_{ji}(t) \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(t) \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}(t) = f^k_\gamma(t) / m\)</span>:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Temporal part: <span class="math inline">\(f^0_\gamma(t) = 0\)</span> (<span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{F}_\gamma\)</span> is spatial) and <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^0_{ji}(t) = 0\)</span> give <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U}(t) = 0\)</span>, consistent with <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U}(t) = 1\)</span>: it carries no information.</p></li>
<li><p>Spatial part: splitting the sum over <span class="math inline">\(i, j\)</span> into temporal and spatial values, and using <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta} = \Gamma^\alpha_{\beta0}\)</span> (torsion-free),  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
                    \underbrace{\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U}(t)
                    + \Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\delta}(t) \, \dot{\gamma}^\beta_\mathcal{U}(t) \, \dot{\gamma}^\delta_\mathcal{U}(t)
                    + 2 \, \Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta}(t) \, \dot{\gamma}^\beta_\mathcal{U}(t)
                    + \Gamma^\alpha_{00}(t)}_{a^\alpha_\gamma}
                    = \frac{f^\alpha_\gamma(t)}{m}.
                \end{align*}</span></p></li>
</ol>
<p>Only the whole left-hand side is a component function of the vector field <span class="math inline">\(a_\gamma\)</span> along <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span>; the individual terms are not, since the connection coefficient functions are not the component functions of a tensor field. Moved to the right-hand side and multiplied by <span class="math inline">\(m\)</span>, each <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>-term looks like an additional force, called a <strong>pseudo-force</strong>, which a change of stratified chart can create or remove.</p></li>
</ul>
<section class="dg-footnotes" role="doc-endnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-4" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-4" aria-label="Back to the text">4</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Given any chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> around <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\((dt)_p \neq 0\)</span> implies <span class="math inline">\(\partial_\kappa \left[ t \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) \neq 0\)</span> for some <span class="math inline">\(\kappa\)</span>. Replacing <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^\kappa\)</span> by <span class="math inline">\(\left. t \right|_\mathcal{U}\)</span> as zeroth coordinate gives a transition map with Jacobian determinant <span class="math inline">\(\pm \partial_\kappa \left[ t \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big) \neq 0\)</span>, hence, by the inverse function theorem, a chart around <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> in the maximal atlas. <span class="math inline">\(\square\)</span></p></div></div></section>
